result:
There is a particular quality to the hour just before dawn, when the world has not yet decided what kind of day it will be. Streetlights still hold their small territories of amber, but the sky has begun to thin, shifting from black to a color with no proper name—something between slate and the inside of a shell. Sound travels differently then. A single car at the far end of the road seems both nearer and more distant than it should, its engine a low thread pulled through the quiet.

I have always liked this threshold more than the sunrise itself. Sunrise is a performance; the pre-dawn is a rehearsal no one was invited to watch. Birds begin their arguments one voice at a time, testing the air. Somewhere a sprinkler starts, ticks, and stops, as if reconsidering. The mind is less defended then. Thoughts arrive without their usual costumes. A worry that felt enormous at midnight looks merely factual. A plan that seemed brilliant looks merely possible.

It is easy to romanticize such hours and harder to protect them. Most of modern life is engineered against unstructured attention. Notifications, schedules, the low hum of other people’s urgency—all of it crowds the edges until the center disappears. Yet the center is where anything worth keeping gets made: a sentence, a decision, a kindness that is not performed for anyone else.

So I try, when I can, to meet the morning before it meets me. Not to optimize it. Just to notice the color with no name, and let that be enough for a little while.
